feedback: D1: Strong, evidence-led catalogue. You quoted the SQLi concat line, the alg:none branch with Token 2, the MD5 hash, the stored XSS beacon at 02:18:47, the open redirect at 02:21:13, the path traversal at 02:24:02, and the setcookie line showing Secure disabled, almost all with correct OWASP and CWE and a real evidence line, which is exactly how a finding earns full credit. Two real findings are missing: the hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (A02 or A05, CWE-798) is nowhere in the catalogue, and no-token-expiry (CWE-613) is only hinted at inside your JWT row rather than stood up as its own finding, so each cost you its share. The XXE row is thin, you cited only a generic parser-error string at Medium confidence and never pointed at the SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd entity in 04-import-xxe.xml, so it reads as suspicion rather than proof. The decoy is where you lost the most: you named the alg:none branch as the decoy and ruled it Exploitable, but alg:none is a genuine vulnerability honoured by the shared /api/v1/internal service, not the safe construct. The actual decoy was the HS256 verify branch using hash_equals(), which is constant-time and therefore sound, and the safe-but-tempting b64url helpers. You needed to name that construct and prove it safe at the mechanism level, so the decoy row earns nothing. D2: This is your best deliverable. The hops are in order, each PoC is verbatim, and you reconciled SQLi to 02:15:31, the 312-row pull to 02:16:04, and the file read to 02:24:02 with full evidence blocks. Your CVSS vectors are complete and you correctly used A:N not A:H on the SQLi for 9.1, with a justification paragraph rather than a bare number. The chain is incomplete though, it skips the stored XSS at 02:18:47 and the open redirect at 02:21:13 as explicit hops, and it omits the recon at 02:14:08 and the failed guess at 02:14:55, so the narrative jumps straight from data access to file read. Your impact work is good, 312 customers, a stated sampling assumption, roughly 63 million NGN, and the BoltCash six-week window, which is exactly the reward-assumptions approach asked for, though page 7 contradicts itself by first saying 20 records then scaling to 312, so tighten that. D3: A clean, board-ready report. The executive summary is jargon-free and lands on customers and naira, the threat model correctly notes the shared internal API exposure, the chain names the earliest break at SQLi, and your remediation table is ordered by effort against risk reduced, not by raw CVSS, which is precisely what was wanted. The decoy section repeats the D1 error and calls alg:none Exploitable, so the disproved-decoy row earns nothing here too. Your detection stopgaps name specific fields, the login body patterns and the alg:none header, but you gave a qualitative Low for false positives rather than a concrete rate, so that row is only partial. D4: Well done, you answered all four prompts in your own voice, cited ISC2 Canon I and Canon II by number and load-bearing, anchored a sentence to your own finding of 312 exposed records, and invoked the NDPA 2023 duty to notify the NDPC and affected data subjects on high risk. You stopped short of naming the sections by number, section 40 for the 72-hour NDPC notification and section 41 for notifying data subjects, which is the one upgrade that would have made it full marks. The single most important fix: the decoy is the constant-time hash_equals HS256 verify branch, not alg:none, and proving that safe construct correctly while still listing alg:none and the hardcoded secret as real bugs would lift both D1 and D3 substantially.
